source.title: Hierarchical Federated Unlearning for Large Language Models
source.authors: Yisheng Zhong; Zheng-Bang Yang; Zhuangdi Zhu

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some table formatting is flattened, but the main table layouts support the method-to-value assignments used below.
record.tranche_reason: The study applies unlearning methods and reports forgetting and utility metrics, bearing on the unlearning-performance portion of version A. It does not test whether attacks recover the target knowledge.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own unlearning and utility outcomes. It does not test recovery by relearning, activation ablation, quantization, or prompting. Mentioned methods and results attributed to other work are not recorded as findings here. Reported forgetting metrics have no stated chance-level reference, so the scores alone do not establish whether target accuracy is near chance.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes FULM, a federated LoRA-adapter merging scheme for unlearning. It uses RMU and gradient ascent as tools and reports only forget-set and MMLU scores for its own method against merging baselines. It runs no relearning, ablation, quantization or prompting attack, so it cannot show whether unlearning is shallow or robust. The robustness clause is central to version A, and version F would need FULM tested against such attacks. Its numbers are standard method-performance reports, not a test of any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that FULM removes target content while maintaining utility and handles heterogeneous, decentralized requests better than merging baselines. They run no recovery-attack experiments.
record.recipe_differences: Uses RMU for WMDP and gradient ascent for TOFU and MUSE, then federated LoRA adapter merging. The study does not reproduce or test the fine-tuning, activation-ablation, quantization, or prompting recovery procedures in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with dataset and merging method; the paper compares near-iid TOFU with heterogeneous WMDP and Harry Potter tasks and reports different merge-method results.
record.problems: The paper gives no chance-level reference for the Forget metrics, no uncertainty estimates, and no recovery-attack evaluation. Utility values are reported without a consistent unmodified-model comparison in the main tables. The text also contains some formatting and table-extraction artifacts.
record.rows_left_out: Table 4 and Appendix Tables 6–9 report additional intra-cluster, individual-adapter, epoch, and forget-set-size results; they are omitted to keep the record focused on the principal merging evaluations and within the 60-row limit. Table 1–3 and Table 5 results are retained.

untested.parts: Whether simple attacks recover the forgotten knowledge. Only post-unlearning forget and utility scores are reported.
No activation-direction ablation or probing of whether knowledge is retained.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, multilingual or in-context attack.
FULM is not claimed or tested to resist recovery attacks.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T2/tests guess is overturned. Reporting forget and utility scores for a new method is T4 here, because version A's distinguishing content is robustness to attack, which is not evaluated. For reference: FULM brings WMDP-Cyber to 25.82%, roughly 4-choice chance, Bio to 39.05% from 63.71%, and MMLU to 57.25% vs 58.19% pretrained. The record's 'no baseline' notes overlook the Table 5 pretrained row. No uncertainty is reported, and the main experiments use a single model (Zephyr-7B).

versions.untested_parts: The study reports forgetting and utility outcomes, but does not test whether simple attacks recover knowledge after unlearning. It does not state a chance-level reference for the reported Forget metrics, and does not establish that general ability is retained relative to a stated baseline.
No post-unlearning fine-tuning or relearning attack is tested.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis establishing blocked access rather than deletion is reported. RMU training perturbs activations, but the study does not test ablation-based recovery.
No prompt rephrasing, jailbreak, language variation, or in-context recovery attack is tested.
FULM is proposed for federated unlearning, but the study does not test its resistance to the recovery attacks in the claim.
